summary: This program asks you to type a temperature in Celsius, converts it to Fahrenheit, and prints the result. The conversion is wrapped in a try-catch block so that typing something that is not a number produces a friendly message instead of a crash.

lines.text: Using print instead of println leaves the cursor on the same line, so what you type appears right after the prompt.
The try block guards everything inside it against errors, and declaring the Scanner in the parentheses (a try-with-resources) closes it automatically when the block ends.
The typed line is read as text, trim removes any stray spaces, and parseDouble turns it into a number — this is the step that fails if the text is not numeric.
The conversion itself lives in its own function, so main stays focused on talking to the user.
Joining numbers to text with + builds one readable sentence out of both values.
If anything inside the try throws, control jumps here; catching the broad Exception type is the simplest starting point, and later exercises narrow it down.

lines.code: System.out.println("Invalid input. Please enter a numeric temperature value.");
lines.text: The reader gets a clear explanation of what went wrong rather than a stack trace, and the program ends normally.
A static helper function can be called straight from main without creating an object, and it returns a double because temperatures have decimals.
This is the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit formula; because celsius is a double, the multiplication and division stay decimal instead of being rounded off.
